summary: The developer machine has the Python runtime, the DocumentDB MCP server, and many DocumentDB agent skills installed; Microsoft Learn documentation is available. The build can start now using the live M30 cluster and the installed skills, but several cold answers were partially wrong (resource types, CLI groups, connection-string shape, vector-index syntax, engine identity). Missing CLI tools (azd, bicep, terraform, mongosh, dotnet) and a few unanswered engineering choices (Python major version, sync vs async driver, LLM/model choices and embedding dims, sample-data size/schema choices) are gaps the builder must pick or add workarounds for. No single unavailable required tool blocks the build; proceed after the builder confirms a few design choices and (optionally) installs small developer tools.
summary_points: Build can start now: python, pip (virtualenv), node/npm, docker, az, documentdb MCP server and Microsoft Learn MCP server are available, and a vector-capable M30 cluster is reachable via DOCUMENTDB_URI.

Many DocumentDB-specific skills are installed (connection, driver, indexing, vector search, local-deployment, natural-language querying), so authoring code and verifying queries/explain plans against the cluster is supported.

Several cold answers were incorrect or outdated: the correct ARM resource type is Microsoft.DocumentDB/mongoClusters (not databaseAccounts), CLI group is az documentdb mongocluster, and connection strings and vector-index creation use the DocumentDB-specific formats and host suffixes shown in Learn.

Missing local developer tools (mongosh) and optional IaC tooling (azd, bicep, terraform, dotnet) are not blockers but would speed verification or alternate workflows; add them if the builder wants a smoother experience.
There are information gaps the builder must resolve (Python major version, sync vs async driver choice, which LLM/embedding model and dims to use, and the sample-data schema/scale).
Verdict: ready_with_gaps — proceed with workarounds and pick defaults for the few unspecified engineering choices.

tools.name: python
tools.needed_for: Run the sample app, virtualenv, run seed scripts, LangChain orchestrator, and tests.
tools.impact_if_missing: Can't run the sample code or tests.
tools.workaround: Install a supported Python runtime (3.10/3.11 recommended). Use a containerized environment if local install isn't possible.

tools.name: pip / virtualenv (via python)
tools.needed_for: Install dependencies (pymongo, langchain, openai/azure-openai client, etc.)
tools.detail: Assumed available with Python virtualenv; inventory notes python and pip work in the virtualenv.
tools.workaround: Use docker to run a container with Python and pip to run the sample.

tools.name: node / npm / npx
tools.needed_for: Optional: run MCP tooling, add skills, or run any Node-based verification/sample scripts. npx may be used to add agent skills if needed.
tools.impact_if_missing: Cannot run Node-based utilities or quickly install MCP skill packages via npx.
tools.workaround: Use Python-based tooling or the installed MCP servers; npx is present so you can add skills if needed.

tools.name: docker
tools.needed_for: Optional local DocumentDB gateway/container for isolated integration tests or reproducible local runs.
tools.impact_if_missing: Can't run a local DocumentDB gateway; must test against live cluster.
tools.workaround: Test against the provided live cluster as the run environment instructs.

tools.name: az (Azure CLI)
tools.needed_for: Inspect Azure resources, view cluster metadata, firewall rules, or perform admin tasks if needed (but run policy forbids writes).
tools.detail: Azure CLI installed and signed in (inventory: az login available).
tools.impact_if_missing: Less convenient to inspect Azure resource metadata or adjust firewall/private endpoints.
tools.workaround: Use the documentdb MCP server for data-plane checks and Learn docs for command syntax.

tools.name: documentdb MCP server (documentdb)
tools.needed_for: Data-plane operations: list databases/collections, sample documents, run aggregation pipelines, create/list indexes, explain plans, and insert the scenario run audit docs to the sample database.

tools.workaround: Use direct PyMongo client to the cluster, but the documentdb MCP server simplifies inspection and explain output formatting.

tools.needed_for: Authoritative documentation search and fetch for verifying API shapes, CLI groups, index creation syntax, auth modes, and vector-search details.

tools.needed_for: Design guidance (index shapes, connection tuning, vector search) and code-level best practices for building the sample and verifying queries and indexes against the cluster.
tools.detail: Many DocumentDB skills are installed per inventory: documentdb-connection, documentdb-driver, documentdb-indexing, documentdb-vector-search, documentdb-natural-language-querying, documentdb-local-deployment, documentdb-mcp-setup, documentdb-data-modeling, documentdb-query-optimizer, etc.

tools.needed_for: Manual interactive checks of connectivity, indexes, and ad-hoc aggregation pipelines during development/verification.
tools.impact_if_missing: Harder for developers to run quick manual queries locally; must use the documentdb MCP server or PyMongo scripts for ad-hoc checks.
tools.workaround: Use PyMongo scripts or the documentdb MCP server's find/aggregate/list-indexes tools to inspect the cluster from the agent.

confusions.question: What is the Azure resource provider namespace and resource type of an Azure DocumentDB cluster?
confusions.cold_answer: Azure resource provider namespace: Microsoft.DocumentDB. Resource type for a cluster/account: Microsoft.DocumentDB/databaseAccounts (child resources like MongoDB databases/collections are under that account).
confusions.grounded_answer: The current first-class resource type for the managed MongoDB-compatible service is Microsoft.DocumentDB/mongoClusters (resource name 'mongoClusters' under the Microsoft.DocumentDB provider).

grounding_links.title: Microsoft.DocumentDB mongoClusters 2024-07-01 (deployment-language-terraform)

confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: Historically the Cosmos DB account resource (Microsoft.DocumentDB/databaseAccounts) hosted MongoDB-compatible APIs; the service surface was reorganised and a distinct 'mongoClusters' resource type now represents vCore clusters.
confusions.build_risk: If the builder used databaseAccounts in ARM/Bicep/CLI examples they would target the Cosmos DB account path rather than the mongoClusters resource and provisioning or ARM-based queries would fail or act on the wrong service.
improvements: Document the new resource type prominently on the Quickstart and 'create cluster' pages (Learn quickstart and CLI docs) so readers don't default to 'databaseAccounts'.
Add a clear note on any legacy pages that references Microsoft.DocumentDB/databaseAccounts pointing to 'mongoClusters' for vCore clusters.

confusions.question: Which Azure CLI command group creates and manages a cluster? Is it in the core CLI or an extension?
confusions.cold_answer: Use the core CLI group az cosmosdb. Example to create: az cosmosdb create --name my-docdb-account --resource-group my-rg --locations regionName=westus --default-consistency-level Strong --kind MongoDB. (az cosmosdb is part of the core az CLI, not a separate extension.)
confusions.grounded_answer: The correct command group for the vCore-managed DocumentDB clusters is az documentdb mongocluster (az documentdb mongocluster create, az documentdb mongocluster list, etc.).

grounding_links.title: az documentdb mongocluster create (Azure CLI docs)
Quickstart: Create an Azure DocumentDB cluster by using Azure CLI

confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: Both services historically shared the Microsoft.DocumentDB namespace and both expose MongoDB-compatible endpoints; older Cosmos DB (databaseAccounts) CLI docs and examples use az cosmosdb while the new managed clusters use az documentdb mongocluster.
confusions.build_risk: If the builder runs az cosmosdb commands they will manage Cosmos DB accounts (RU model) rather than provisioning or managing the vCore mongoClusters; CLI commands will fail or touch a different resource.
improvements: Add a cross-link at the top of the az cosmosdb (and cosmetically similar pages) pointing to az documentdb mongocluster when the intent is vCore-managed MongoDB clusters.
Add an explicit CLI quickstart header line: 'To manage vCore DocumentDB clusters use az documentdb mongocluster (not az cosmosdb).' on the quickstart docs.

confusions.question: Which Bicep and Terraform resource types deploy a cluster?
confusions.cold_answer: Bicep/ARM: resource type Microsoft.DocumentDB/databaseAccounts. Terraform (azurerm provider): azurerm_cosmosdb_account.
confusions.grounded_answer: To deploy the managed vCore cluster you should use Microsoft.DocumentDB/mongoClusters (ARM/Bicep) or the corresponding Terraform/AzAPI resource that targets microsoft.documentdb/mongoClusters (or use the Azure Verified Module for Cosmos DB for MongoDB (vCore) if available).

grounding_links.title: Microsoft.DocumentDB mongoClusters 2024-07-01 (deployment-language-terraform)

confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: Older ARM/Terraform examples for Cosmos DB used the databaseAccounts path; vCore clusters were introduced as a separate top-level resource type (mongoClusters).
confusions.build_risk: Using the wrong ARM resource type in IaC will either fail deployment or create a different (Cosmos DB RU) account; the sample must use mongoClusters when referencing the vCore cluster.
improvements: Update any IaC quickstarts or repo templates that still use databaseAccounts to either include an explicit example for mongoClusters or mark which resource to pick for vCore clusters.

confusions.question: What does a connection string look like: scheme, host suffix, port, and the options it must carry?
confusions.cold_answer: Typical MongoDB-compatible connection string: either mongodb:// or mongodb+srv://. Hostname pattern: <account-name>.mongo.cosmos.azure.com (or <account>.documents.azure.com for some accounts); common port is 10255 for TLS. Example: mongodb://myUser:myPassword@myaccount.mongo.cosmos.azure.com:10255/?ssl=true&replicaSet=globaldb&retryWrites=false.
confusions.grounded_answer: DocumentDB vCore clusters expose connection strings via az documentdb mongocluster list-connection-strings (or the portal) and commonly return SRV or standard URIs that look like mongodb+srv://<user>:<password>@<cluster-name>.global.mongocluster.cosmos.azure.com/...?tls=true&authMechanism=MONGODB-OIDC (when using AAD) or SCRAM options for native auth. Port 10255 is a legacy Cosmos DB for MongoDB endpoint; the managed mongoClusters use the host suffix and options shown in the cluster's list-connection-strings output (SRV form with .global.mongocluster.cosmos.azure.com in examples).

grounding_links.title: Quickstart: Create an Azure DocumentDB cluster by using Azure CLI
Get-AzDocumentDBMongoClusterConnectionString (PowerShell docs example output)

confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: The cold answer quoted connection-string shapes and ports that match the older Cosmos DB (RU) Mongo endpoints and community Cosmos examples (which used 10255). The vCore-managed mongoClusters return SRV and URI formats with the 'mongocluster.cosmos.azure.com' suffix and may provide OIDC parameters for Entra auth.

confusion_sources.title: Older Cosmos DB MongoDB connection string examples (databaseAccounts pages)

confusions.build_risk: Using the wrong host suffix or port could fail to connect or connect to a different service; building code that hardcodes 10255 or replicaSet=globaldb will mis-handle SRV URIs and Microsoft Entra ID auth flows.
improvements: Clarify connection-string examples on quickstarts and signal when SRV form is returned; add an explicit example for Microsoft's managed mongoClusters including MONGODB-OIDC/Entra examples and the SRV host suffix.

confusions.question: How is capacity provisioned and billed: request units, compute tiers with vCores, serverless, or something else?
confusions.cold_answer: Capacity is typically provisioned as a managed cluster tier (named tiers like M10/M30 etc. in this environment) priced by compute (vCores/instance class) plus storage; it is not the Cosmos DB RU model for this MongoDB-compatible offering. There may also be serverless or autoscale flavors in some SKUs, but for this sample you should use the M30 compute tier as provided.
confusions.grounded_answer: Correct: Azure DocumentDB (vCore managed MongoDB-compatible service) is billed by compute (cluster tier in M-series, vCores/memory per shard) and storage; it does not use the Cosmos DB RU model. See pricing guidance and 'compute and storage' docs.

grounding_links.title: Azure DocumentDB pricing explained

confusions.question: Which authentication methods are supported, and how does a driver authenticate with Microsoft Entra ID?
confusions.cold_answer: Primary supported data-plane auth methods: standard MongoDB username/password (SCRAM-SHA-1 or SCRAM-SHA-256) and TLS/X.509 client certificate auth when enabled. Some managed offerings also support Azure AD (Microsoft Entra) token-based auth, but that typically requires obtaining an Azure AD access token and supplying it to the driver (using the driver SASL/OAUTHBEARER or passing the token as the password depending on driver support). In practice for immediate coding use, use the provided username/password credential in the connection string (SCRAM) or a client X.509 cert. If using Azure AD, obtain an access token for the service principal and pass it to the driver per the provider documentation (this flow is provider-specific).
confusions.grounded_answer: Azure DocumentDB supports native (SCRAM) authentication and Microsoft Entra ID (OIDC) authentication. Entra-based auth is implemented via OIDC for clients: applications present an Entra-issued OIDC access token and (for many clients) use a connection string param such as authMechanism=MONGODB-OIDC or use the driver's OIDC support; the cluster can be configured to allow NativeAuth, MicrosoftEntraID, or both.

grounding_links.title: Connect to Azure DocumentDB using role-based access control and Microsoft Entra ID

confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: The cold answer was generic (token-as-password or SASL/OAUTHBEARER) but the authoritative doc specifies OIDC (MONGODB-OIDC / authMechanism) and cluster auth modes, so the actual mechanism and driver configuration are more specific than the cold answer implied.
confusions.build_risk: If the builder implements Entra auth using an ad-hoc token-to-password approach they may not match the driver's expected MONGODB-OIDC mechanism and the connection will fail.
improvements: Add a short example in the 'how-to-connect-role-based-access-control' page showing the client-side connection string and a PyMongo/driver snippet for Entra (MONGODB-OIDC) authentication.
In driver best-practices (documentdb-driver skill) add explicit guidance and a snippet for acquiring an OIDC token and passing it to a supported driver or using authMechanism=MONGODB-OIDC.

confusions.question: Which client library should an application use? Is there a service-specific SDK?
confusions.cold_answer: For data-plane access use standard MongoDB drivers (for Python: pymongo or motor). There is no special proprietary data-plane SDK required for MongoDB-compatible DocumentDB clusters; for management you can use azure-cli/azure-sdk management libraries (azure-mgmt-cosmosdb or azure-native in IaC).
confusions.grounded_answer: Correct: use standard MongoDB drivers (PyMongo / motor) for data-plane operations. Management plane uses Azure CLI / Azure management SDKs. There is no unique data-plane SDK for DocumentDB — standard Mongo drivers are the right choice.

grounding_links.title: Quickstart: Connect MongoDB EF Core Provider to Azure DocumentDB (prerequisites mentions native DB user and drivers)

confusions.question: Which vector index types are supported, and what does the command that creates one look like?
confusions.cold_answer: Supported vector index methods in MongoDB-7-style syntax: HNSW, IVF, DiskANN (depending on cluster build). Create example (Mongo shell / pymongo): db.positions.createIndex( { embedding: 'knnVector' }, { name: 'embedding_knn', 'knnVector': { 'dimensions': 1536, 'method': 'hnsw', 'similarity': 'cosine', 'efConstruction': 200, 'M': 16 } } ). For DiskANN or IVF replace method:'diskann' or method:'ivf' and supply method-specific params.
confusions.grounded_answer: Azure DocumentDB supports IVF, HNSW, and DiskANN vector indexes. The service uses its createIndexes/createSearchIndexes templates or the 'cosmosSearch' / 'vector-<kind>' options (e.g., kind:'vector-diskann', or cosmosSearchOptions with kind:'vector-ivf'). The exact create-index JSON differs from the MongoDB community 'knnVector' key — use the DocumentDB create-index payload (cosmosSearch/cosmosSearchOptions or 'vector-diskann' / 'vector-hnsw' / 'vector-ivf' kinds).

grounding_links.title: Integrated vector store in Azure DocumentDB (vector-search)
Example using an HNSW index (vector-search examples)

confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: The cold answer used a MongoDB/knnVector createIndex syntax that resembles community or Atlas/feature variants; DocumentDB has its own vector-index JSON payload and uses 'cosmosSearch' or 'vector-<kind>' parameters.

confusion_sources.title: Integrated vector store in Azure DocumentDB (vector-search)

confusions.build_risk: If the builder attempts to create a vector index using community 'knnVector' syntax, the cluster will reject it; the app must call the DocumentDB create-index API with the correct 'kind' and options.
improvements: Add a small 'create index' example for Python (PyMongo) in the Vector Search docs that the sample can copy; show both IVF/HNSW/DiskANN examples and the minimal required keys (dimensions, similarity).
Document which cluster tiers permit DiskANN/HNSW vs IVF on the quickstart vector-search pages (already present but make them more prominent).

confusions.question: How are full-text search and hybrid search done?
confusions.cold_answer: Simple full‑text: use MongoDB text indexes (db.collection.createIndex({ field: 'text' })) for basic text search. For advanced hybrid vector+text retrieval use the engine's integrated search if available (a $search/$searchMeta aggregation stage in Atlas-style deployments) or combine vector similarity queries with text scoring in application logic. On Azure you can also integrate with Azure Cognitive Search for richer hybrid search scenarios if the managed Mongo-compatible engine does not provide a Lucene-style search stage.
confusions.grounded_answer: DocumentDB provides integrated search features: use createSearchIndexes and the $search aggregation stage (cosmosSearch operator) for full-text and hybrid search. The service recommends using the integrated search pipeline (createSearchIndexes / $search) rather than community $text, and it supports hybrid flows combining text and vector scoring via the $search stage. Azure Cognitive Search is an optional external integration but not required for DocumentDB integrated search scenarios.

grounding_links.title: Build RAG applications / create a vector index (search & hybrid guidance)
Integrated vector store in Azure DocumentDB (vector-search)

confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: The cold answer suggested community text indexes ($text) and Atlas-style $search semantics; DocumentDB prefers createSearchIndexes and the integrated $search pipeline (cosmosSearch) and provides integrated hybrid capabilities.
confusions.build_risk: If the builder relies on $text indexes and expects DocumentDB to treat them the same as its integrated search, they may see lower functionality or miss built-in hybrid scoring features.
improvements: On the quickstarts, emphasise 'use createSearchIndexes and the $search stage' and show one minimal example for combining vector and lexical signals.

confusions.question: Which MongoDB wire protocol or server versions are supported, and which commonly used MongoDB features are not?
confusions.cold_answer: This cluster advertises MongoDB 7.0 wire protocol compatibility. Commonly restricted or different features on managed Mongo-compatible services include: server-side JavaScript ($where), some admin/diagnostic commands, custom storage-engine options, and in certain SKUs multi-document transactions or certain change-stream/topology features can be limited. Expect standard CRUD, aggregation pipeline, and new vector index features to work, but verify unsupported commands in the service docs or by testing.
confusions.grounded_answer: DocumentDB supports multiple MongoDB wire-protocol versions (including 5.0, 6.0, 7.0 and in many clusters 8.0 compatibility as documented per cluster/server-version). Some server-side features and admin commands are restricted; check service-specific docs for exact supported commands. The precise supported server versions are declared on the cluster (serverVersion option) and can vary; for this sample the cluster is said to advertise MongoDB 7.0 wire protocol compatibility in the run environment.

grounding_links.title: Compare Azure DocumentDB to MongoDB Atlas (supported wire versions list)

confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: The cold answer was cautious but incomplete: the service supports multiple wire-protocol versions and documents the precise supported versions; saying simply 'advertises 7.0' misses the full set and the per-cluster configurable serverVersion.
confusions.build_risk: If the builder assumes only 7.0 is supported when a different serverVersion is selected on the cluster, some driver features or aggregation stages could mismatch.
improvements: Add a short table to the quickstart noting 'serverVersion: supported wire protocols (5/6/7/8) and how to choose or query serverVersion on the cluster'.

confusions.question: How do you run the database locally for development and tests: which image or emulator, and which port?
confusions.cold_answer: There is no perfect official Azure-native local emulator for the MongoDB-compatible cluster. For local development run the official MongoDB docker image (e.g. mongo:7.0) and bind to port 27017: docker run --rm -p 27017:27017 --name local-mongo mongo:7.0. Use that for running aggregation and vector logic locally if the server supports the same features; otherwise test against the live cluster.
confusions.grounded_answer: DocumentDB provides a Gateway Docker image for local development and the agent kit references a gateway that exposes MongoDB on port 10260 and mentions port 10260 for the Gateway and TLS/SCRAM-SHA-256 config. For full parity, the skill recommends the Gateway image (not simply mongo:7.0) because it mirrors DocumentDB features such as vector/index behaviours and security defaults.

grounding_links.title: documentdb-local-deployment (skill)

confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: The cold answer assumed using the stock MongoDB docker image which is convenient, but the DocumentDB local gateway image and port (10260) better mirror the managed cluster's behaviour and features.
confusions.build_risk: Using stock mongo:7.0 (27017) for local tests may fail to exercise DocumentDB-specific features (gateway behaviour, vector-index implementations, TLS and auth options), causing surprises when running against the live cluster.
improvements: Document the Gateway Docker image and default port (10260) more prominently in local development quickstarts and the documentdb-local-deployment skill instructions.

confusions.question: Are change streams supported, and does anything have to be enabled first?
confusions.cold_answer: Change streams (watch()) are supported on replica-set style MongoDB clusters; on managed MongoDB-compatible offerings they are often available but may require an appropriate SKU/tier and that the deployment maintain an oplog. No extra client-side enablement is normally required beyond using a driver that supports watch() and connecting with a user that has read privileges. Verify by running db.collection.watch() in your environment.
confusions.grounded_answer: Correct: DocumentDB supports change streams. For multishard clusters there is a preview feature to enable multi-shard change streams; for general use change streams are available but features like multishard or historical replay require enabling specific cluster features. Some features (pre-images, pre/post images) need enabling on the collection.

grounding_links.title: Change streams in Azure DocumentDB

confusions.question: Which MCP server gives an agent data-plane tools for this service? Does the general Azure MCP Server cover it?
confusions.cold_answer: Use the documentdb-specific MCP server (documentdb) to get MongoDB-aware data-plane tooling and inspection (the environment statement references a 'documentdb' MCP server). The generic Azure MCP server may not include MongoDB-specific helpers (index/model inspectors, explain plan viewers) so prefer the documentdb MCP server for data-plane operations.
confusions.grounded_answer: Correct: the 'documentdb' MCP server provides data-plane tools tailored for Azure DocumentDB; the generic Azure MCP server exists for control-plane tasks but doesn't replace documentdb's data-plane helpers.

grounding_links.title: documentdb MCP server (inventory)

confusions.question: What was this service called before, and how does it relate to Azure Cosmos DB and to the open-source DocumentDB project?
confusions.cold_answer: Historically Microsoft had an internal DocumentDB offering that evolved into Azure Cosmos DB; 'DocumentDB' is an older Microsoft name and is distinct from the open-source 'DocumentDB' projects elsewhere. The current managed MongoDB-compatible service is a separate managed offering (exposed via Microsoft.DocumentDB provider for ARM) that provides a MongoDB wire-compatible endpoint; it is not the same as the old DocumentDB SQL API but is related in the Azure ecosystem.
confusions.grounded_answer: Partly right but imprecise: the vCore-managed MongoDB-compatible service was previously named 'vCore-based Azure Cosmos DB for MongoDB' and has been rebranded as 'Azure DocumentDB' to align with the open-source DocumentDB engine. It is distinct from Cosmos DB's RU-based MongoDB API and from Amazon DocumentDB; it is built on the open-source DocumentDB engine.

grounding_links.title: Azure DocumentDB FAQ and relation to Azure Cosmos DB

confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: Naming has changed over time: 'DocumentDB' was an older Microsoft Cosmos offering and 'vCore-based Cosmos DB for MongoDB' was a previous marketing name. The rebrand and the open-source DocumentDB engine create overlapping names that cause confusion.
confusions.build_risk: Writers or samples that say 'use az cosmosdb' or target Cosmos DB RU accounts may be pointing users to the wrong service.
improvements: Add a short 'how this differs from Cosmos DB for MongoDB (RU) and Amazon DocumentDB' section at the top of the quickstart and FAQ pages to remove ambiguity.

confusions.question: What engine is underneath, and does that change anything in application code?
confusions.cold_answer: Underneath is a MongoDB‑compatible engine (either a MongoDB-compatible server implementation provided by the service or a MongoDB distribution). From an application perspective you should use standard MongoDB drivers and the MongoDB wire protocol; most CRUD/aggregation code is unchanged. However some server-side features, admin commands, and edge-case behaviors may differ, so test features like transactions, server-side JS, and certain aggregation stages against the target cluster.
confusions.grounded_answer: The service runs on the open-source DocumentDB engine (the open-source DocumentDB project) that provides MongoDB compatibility. From an application perspective you still use standard MongoDB drivers and the MongoDB wire protocol, but the engine is not the MongoDB server itself — some admin commands and rare server-side behaviors can differ and must be verified. This distinction matters when assuming exact parity with MongoDB server implementations.

grounding_links.title: Moving from another MongoDB-compatible service to Azure DocumentDB (engine and compatibility)

confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: The cold answer assumed 'MongoDB server' underneath; in reality DocumentDB runs its own open-source DocumentDB engine that implements MongoDB compatibility. The practical effect for app code is usually minimal, but the distinction matters for licensing and for admin commands/edge-case compatibility.
confusions.build_risk: If the builder assumes exact binary parity with MongoDB server and relies on unsupported admin commands or behaviors, tests may fail during verification or in production.
improvements: Add a clear sentence in the quickstarts and driver best-practices: 'Use MongoDB drivers; the engine is DocumentDB (open source) and not the upstream MongoDB server—test specialized server-side features explicitly.'

confusions.question: What collection and index definitions will the sample create for positions and embeddings?
confusions.cold_answer: Create a positions collection and indexes: 1) standard compound index on accountId and instrumentId for fast lookups: db.positions.createIndex({ accountId: 1, instrumentId: 1 }) 2) vector knn index on embedding field (example 1536-dim, HNSW): db.positions.createIndex({ embedding: 'knnVector' }, { name: 'embedding_knn', knnVector: { dimensions: 1536, method: 'hnsw', similarity: 'cosine', efConstruction: 200, M: 16 } })
confusions.grounded_answer: The positions collection and a compound filter index are sensible. For vector indexes, DocumentDB expects the service-specific create-index payload (e.g., createSearchIndexes/cosmosSearchOptions or a 'vector-<kind>' index via its API). Do not rely on 'knnVector' community syntax; instead use the DocumentDB vector-index construction (kind:'vector-hnsw' / 'vector-diskann' / 'vector-ivf' with dimensions and method-specific params).

grounding_links.title: Integrated vector store in Azure DocumentDB (vector-search)

confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: The cold answer used community/Atlas-style knnVector index syntax that won't be accepted by DocumentDB; the correct shape uses DocumentDB's vector index format and the cosmosSearch operator.
confusions.build_risk: Using the wrong createIndex syntax will cause index creation to fail; the builder must call the DocumentDB create-index API with the correct options.
improvements: Include a minimal Python snippet in the sample repo that demonstrates creating the vector index using the DocumentDB create-index API (or via the MCP 'documentdb_create_index' tool) so builders copy the right payload.

information_gaps.title: Python major/version choice
information_gaps.description: Prompt and installed skills do not specify which Python major version to target. Inventory shows Python 3.13 is present, but many libraries (LangChain, PyMongo pinned versions) test against 3.10/3.11. The builder must decide and pin dependencies accordingly; I checked the prompt_review and the installed skills but found no authoritative version requirement.

information_gaps.title: Driver sync vs async design
information_gaps.description: No skill or doc prescribes whether the sample should use synchronous PyMongo or async (motor / AsyncIOMotorClient). documentdb-connection discusses tuning but doesn't mandate sync vs async for LangChain multi-agent patterns. The builder must pick a model and adapt connection-pooling guidance from the documentdb-connection and documentdb-driver skills.

information_gaps.title: LLM provider and embedding model/dimensions
information_gaps.description: The prompt asks for a LangChain multi-agent system but does not name an LLM provider or embedding model. The DocumentDB vector index dims must match the chosen embedding model (e.g., 1536 for OpenAI text-embedding-3-small). No installed skill or doc in the inventory prescribes a default model for samples; the builder must choose and document it.

information_gaps.title: Sample data schema and size
information_gaps.description: No authoritative sample dataset or schema is provided for 'positions'. The prompt-review suggested a plausible schema but the builder must author seed data and decide record counts to keep costs reasonable; the documentdb-local-deployment and data-modeling skills provide guidance but no concrete seed dataset was found.

information_gaps.title: App surface (CLI vs API vs web)

inventory_recommendations.name: azd
inventory_recommendations.recommendation: Not required for this sample (no provisioning). If the team wants to support 'azd' authoring and deploy-to-azure templates as part of CI, install azd; otherwise document that provisioning is out of scope.

inventory_recommendations.name: bicep
inventory_recommendations.recommendation: Not required to build the sample (the run policy forbids Azure writes). Add bicep if the repo will include Bicep IaC for cluster provisioning; otherwise the sample should include a comment that Bicep/Terraform provisioning is optional.

inventory_recommendations.name: terraform
inventory_recommendations.recommendation: Not required for this sample. If maintainers want Terraform IaC artifacts in the repo for optional provisioning, install terraform and add a README note. Otherwise skip installation.

inventory_recommendations.name: mongosh
inventory_recommendations.recommendation: Useful for manual interactive debugging and ad-hoc verification (inspect indexes, run aggregation pipelines). Install mongosh on PATH (recommended) so developers can quickly connect to the cluster; otherwise use PyMongo scripts or the documentdb MCP server's find/aggregate tools.
